- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").

\begin{abstract}
Compound sparsity---simultaneously pruning attention heads and evicting KV cache entries---is essential for efficient LLM inference but produces super-additive quality degradation whose structure is poorly understood.
Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as approximately constant across the generation process.
We show that this assumption is wrong: compound sparsity severity is an emergent phase-strategy interaction that varies by over an order of magnitude across reasoning phases.

We evaluate compound sparsity on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (both Qwen2 architecture, 7B parameters) using 50 MATH-500 problems, measuring the Interaction Index---a super-additivity metric---across quantile-segmented reasoning phases at sparsity levels $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low-sparsity and high-sparsity reasoning phases increases monotonically from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$, with paired Cohen's $d_z$ growing from $0.44$ (small) to $0.80$ (large); Bonferroni-corrected permutation tests yield $p < 0.005$ at all four sparsity levels.
Random eviction produces no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) shows negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$), confirming that the severity gradient is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.
At $s{=}0.25$, a crossover emerges: importance-based eviction outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.
The pattern replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z \geq 0.55$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$).

We propose entropy-discrimination collapse as an explanatory mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is already broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
These findings challenge the phase-invariance assumption in compound sparsity deployment and motivate phase-aware compression budgets for reasoning models.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Long-context language models place acute pressure on the key--value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length \cite{kwon-sosp2023, pope-mlsys2023}.
Two complementary responses---\emph{attention head pruning} \cite{voita-acl2019, michel-neurips2019} and \emph{KV cache eviction} \cite{snapkv-neurips2024, adakv-neurips2025}---can be deployed simultaneously as \emph{compound sparsity}, but the resulting quality degradation is often super-additive \cite{spark-aaai2026, slim-icml2025}.

Prior work treats compound interaction magnitude as roughly constant across generation \cite{spark-aaai2026, unicomp-2026}.
This assumption is problematic for reasoning models, whose generations alternate between broadly distributed attention (exploratory reasoning) and sharply concentrated attention (structured computation) \cite{thinkv-iclr2026, decision-repr-transition-2026}.
If compound severity varies across these phases, a uniform sparsity budget may be safe in one phase yet destructive in another.

We show that compound sparsity severity is strongly modulated by reasoning phase and eviction strategy.
Under importance-based KV cache eviction, the Interaction Index---a measure of super-additive degradation---concentrates in low-sparsity phases and is largely absent in high-sparsity phases.
On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, the median phase difference rises from $0.39$ at $s{=}0.15$ to $14.59$ at $s{=}0.30$ ($d_z$: $0.44 \to 0.80$; Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all levels).
The pattern replicates at $s \geq 0.20$ on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct ($d_z \geq 0.55$).
Critically, random eviction produces no such gradient (7/8 conditions non-significant), confirming the gradient is an emergent phase-strategy interaction.

We propose \emph{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanism: head pruning flattens cumulative importance scores in phases where attention is broadly distributed, degrading the discriminative power of importance-based eviction in a phase-dependent manner.
Random eviction is immune because its decisions are independent of attention patterns.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item We identify a \textbf{phase--strategy interaction}: importance-based eviction exhibits a severity gradient across reasoning phases that is absent under random eviction (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We show this gradient \textbf{increases monotonically with sparsity} and replicates across two models with different training regimes (\S\ref{sec:results}).
    \item We propose \textbf{entropy-discrimination collapse} as a mechanistic explanation (\S\ref{sec:discrimination-collapse}).
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Discrimination Collapse Details}
2	\label{app:discrimination-collapse-details}
3	
4	The \textbf{Gini coefficient} measures inequality in the importance distribution ($\mathrm{Gini}{=}0$: perfectly uniform; $\mathrm{Gini}{=}1$: maximally concentrated). The \textbf{coefficient of variation} (CV) captures relative dispersion. Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics-full} reports both metrics.

7	\centering
8	\caption{Discrimination collapse under importance-based eviction. $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ are post-pruning minus baseline; negative values indicate reduced discriminative power. All 8 conditions show consistent negative deltas across both models.}
9	\label{tab:discrimination-metrics-full}
10	\small
11	\begin{tabular}{llrr}
12	\toprule
13	Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ & $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ \\
14	\midrule

26	\end{table}
27	
28	Under importance-based eviction, the Gini delta is negative at every sparsity level for both models, with magnitude scaling monotonically with sparsity in DeepSeek. The CV delta is likewise negative in all 8 importance-based conditions. The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: $-0.031$ to $-0.073$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.045$), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not of the eviction strategy. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen
29	
30	This cross-model consistency establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-$s$ fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction.
31	
32	
33	\section{Extended Discussion}
34	\label{app:extended-discussion}
35	
36	\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
37	The magnitude of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
38	The compound interaction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to $0.105$ in a supplementary experiment, indicating onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_imp_s035; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053; s035 II_high=0.1051
39	
40	\paragraph{Random masking as falsification control.}
41	If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly, random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient. It does not: random eviction fails 7/8 paired permutation tests across both models; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$). The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
42	
43	\paragraph{Cross-model magnitude asymmetry.}
44	Qwen's median severity differences ($0.04 \to 0.23 \to 1.27 \to 2.94$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ ($d_z{=}0.44$), while Qwen's becomes significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z{=}0.55$). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
45	We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.
46	
47	\paragraph{Architecture generality.}
48	Discrimination collapse depends on: (i)~attention-mass-based importance scoring for KV eviction, and (ii)~a sufficient number of pruned heads to degrade the importance distribution. Both are shared by major KV cache methods (H$_2$O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) and by any autoregressive transformer producing extended reasoning. The entropy redistribution component, while consistent in DeepSeek, appears model-dependent.
49	
50	\paragraph{Testable prediction.}
51	Any importance metric derived from attention mass should exhibit discrimination collapse under head pruning, with severity gradient scaling with pruning-induced Gini decrease. Metrics deriving importance from sources independent of attention---such as activation magnitude or gradient-based saliency---should produce flatter severity gradients.
52	
53	\paragraph{Future directions.}
54	A \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity in real time and dynamically adjusts compound sparsity per phase could mitigate severity amplification while preserving compression gains where compound behavior is near-additive.
55	Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full mechanism.
56	Scaling to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish generality.
57	
58	
59	\section{Extended Limitations}
60	\label{app:limitations}
61	
62	\paragraph{Model scale.}
63	All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
64	Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
65	Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
66	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
67	% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.
68	
69	\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
70	Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
71	The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
72	The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.
73	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
74	% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.
75	
76	\paragraph{Task coverage.}
77	We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
78	Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
79	Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
80	% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
81	% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.
82	
83	\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
84	Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples. The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
85	The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
86	All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.19$ to $6.70$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider (e.g., $[6.70,\; 16.29]$ at $s{=}0.30$), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification. % exp_id: permutation_test_results.json; permutation CIs: s015=[0.19,0.62], s020=[0.69,1.49], s025=[1.66,6.64], s030=[6.70,16.29]
87	
88	A notable exception among the random baselines is the Qwen random condition at $s{=}0.30$, which yields a statistically significant result ($p{=}0.012$) despite negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$, bootstrap CI excluding zero). % exp_id: qw_rand_s030; B=10000, p=0.012, d=-0.035, negligible
89	This case illustrates that dichotomous significance testing can flag effects of no practical magnitude---reinforcing the importance of reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.
90

\section{Discrimination Collapse Details}
\label{app:discrimination-collapse-details}

The \textbf{Gini coefficient} measures inequality in the importance distribution ($\mathrm{Gini}{=}0$: perfectly uniform; $\mathrm{Gini}{=}1$: maximally concentrated). The \textbf{coefficient of variation} (CV) captures relative dispersion. Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics-full} reports both metrics.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Discrimination collapse under importance-based eviction. $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ are post-pruning minus baseline; negative values indicate reduced discriminative power. All 8 conditions show consistent negative deltas across both models.}
\label{tab:discrimination-metrics-full}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llrr}
\toprule
Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ & $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ \\
\midrule
DeepSeek & $0.15$ & $-0.030$ & $-0.56$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.20$ & $-0.040$ & $-0.77$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.25$ & $-0.065$ & $-1.29$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.30$ & $-0.081$ & $-1.66$ \\
\midrule
Qwen & $0.15$ & $-0.010$ & $-0.05$ \\
Qwen & $0.20$ & $-0.012$ & $-0.21$ \\
Qwen & $0.25$ & $-0.010$ & $-1.49$ \\
Qwen & $0.30$ & $-0.020$ & $-1.14$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Under importance-based eviction, the Gini delta is negative at every sparsity level for both models, with magnitude scaling monotonically with sparsity in DeepSeek. The CV delta is likewise negative in all 8 importance-based conditions. The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: $-0.031$ to $-0.073$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.045$), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not of the eviction strategy. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen

This cross-model consistency establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-$s$ fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction.


\section{Extended Discussion}
\label{app:extended-discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
The magnitude of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
The compound interaction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to $0.105$ in a supplementary experiment, indicating onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_imp_s035; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053; s035 II_high=0.1051

\paragraph{Random masking as falsification control.}
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly, random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient. It does not: random eviction fails 7/8 paired permutation tests across both models; the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$). The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)

\paragraph{Cross-model magnitude asymmetry.}
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.04 \to 0.23 \to 1.27 \to 2.94$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ ($d_z{=}0.44$), while Qwen's becomes significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z{=}0.55$). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Architecture generality.}
Discrimination collapse depends on: (i)~attention-mass-based importance scoring for KV eviction, and (ii)~a sufficient number of pruned heads to degrade the importance distribution. Both are shared by major KV cache methods (H$_2$O, SnapKV, PyramidKV) and by any autoregressive transformer producing extended reasoning. The entropy redistribution component, while consistent in DeepSeek, appears model-dependent.

\paragraph{Testable prediction.}
Any importance metric derived from attention mass should exhibit discrimination collapse under head pruning, with severity gradient scaling with pruning-induced Gini decrease. Metrics deriving importance from sources independent of attention---such as activation magnitude or gradient-based saliency---should produce flatter severity gradients.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
A \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity in real time and dynamically adjusts compound sparsity per phase could mitigate severity amplification while preserving compression gains where compound behavior is near-additive.
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full mechanism.
Scaling to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish generality.


\section{Extended Limitations}
\label{app:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.

\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples. The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.19$ to $6.70$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider (e.g., $[6.70,\; 16.29]$ at $s{=}0.30$), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification. % exp_id: permutation_test_results.json; permutation CIs: s015=[0.19,0.62], s020=[0.69,1.49], s025=[1.66,6.64], s030=[6.70,16.29]

A notable exception among the random baselines is the Qwen random condition at $s{=}0.30$, which yields a statistically significant result ($p{=}0.012$) despite negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$, bootstrap CI excluding zero). % exp_id: qw_rand_s030; B=10000, p=0.012, d=-0.035, negligible
This case illustrates that dichotomous significance testing can flag effects of no practical magnitude---reinforcing the importance of reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.

\paragraph{Sparsity range.}
Our experiments span $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets.
More extreme sparsity ($s > 0.50$) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics---the sub-exponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified.
Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Why not test higher sparsity? 0.30 is conservative."
% REBUTTAL: Our focus is on the practically relevant regime where models retain usable quality. At s>0.30 both strategies degrade severely, making II measurement less informative. The sub-exponential growth (C6, $\Delta$ growth rate $3.8{\times} \to 4.8{\times} \to 2.0{\times}$) suggests saturation at higher sparsity, but confirming this is future work.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "No system evaluation. How do we know the severity amplification matters for real deployment?"
% REBUTTAL: This is an empirical finding paper, not a method/system paper. The contribution is characterizing *what happens* (phase-modulated severity) and *why* (entropy-discrimination collapse), not building a system to fix it. Phase-gated controllers are explicitly scoped as future work. The finding is actionable regardless: any compound sparsity deployment should be aware of phase-dependent severity.

\section{Entropy Redistribution Analysis}
\label{app:entropy-redistribution}

Beyond discrimination collapse, we examine whether head pruning also redistributes the attention entropy of surviving heads. We measure the mean attention entropy per head:
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{H}_i^{(h)} = -\sum_{j=1}^{T} a_{ij}^{(h)} \log a_{ij}^{(h)}
    \label{eq:attn-entropy}
\end{equation}
and compute $\Delta\mathcal{H}$ as the change from baseline (no pruning) to the pruned condition.

The mid-sparsity phase contains fewer segments (median~26), which reduces statistical power for that phase; however, the reversal is equally present in the low-sparsity phase with substantially more segments, so mid-phase power limitations are a confound but do not account for the full pattern. We interpret this as a genuine model-specific difference, possibly arising from distinct head specialization patterns: Qwen's instruction tuning (vs.\ DeepSeek's distillation-based training) may produce head configurations where removing 25\% of heads triggers compensatory broadening rather than concentration.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Compound compression.}
Combining multiple compression axes produces non-additive errors.
\cite{spark-aaai2026} report super-additive degradation when combining channel pruning with token eviction; \cite{slim-icml2025} formalize compound error for quantization and sparsity.
\cite{unicomp-2026} evaluate compound compression across 40+ benchmarks, revealing that reasoning capabilities degrade disproportionately.
\cite{phase-transition-compression-2026} characterize independent phase transition points per compression dimension, implying the joint safe region is the intersection of per-dimension safe zones.
GRASPrune~\cite{graspune-acl2026} learns global budget-constrained gates for joint pruning but treats decisions as static across generation.
These works establish compound interaction but share an implicit assumption: interaction magnitude is constant across the generation process.

\paragraph{KV cache eviction.}
Most methods rely on importance scoring whose reliability is increasingly questioned.
Ada-KV~\cite{adakv-neurips2025} introduces per-head adaptive budgets; SnapKV~\cite{snapkv-neurips2024} compresses from a fixed observation window; \cite{defensivekv-iclr2026} show worst-case loss $2.3$--$4.3{\times}$ higher than expected under standard aggregation.
\cite{nacl-acl2024} combine proxy-token and random eviction to counter attention bias.
RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies deferred importance, and \cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} show that single importance metrics exhibit systematic greedy bias.
These conditions are characterized in terms of aggregation or metric choice---not reasoning phase or interaction with head pruning.

\paragraph{Phase-aware inference.}
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} applies different KV strategies per phase but without compound interaction.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} find pruning sensitivity depends on ``silent'' vs.\ ``decisive'' representation phases.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} show pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines; \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across generation stages.
These works establish phase-dependent compression tolerance along single axes.
Our work bridges this by quantifying how compound severity varies across phases and eviction strategies.
